Listen to this article Share The next global economic revolution is already underway, and it is green. Across the world, industries are being redefined, investments redirected, and entirely new professions created. From renewable energy and sustainable agriculture to carbon markets, electric mobility and the circular economy, the transition towards sustainability is reshaping how nations create wealth. The question is not merely if Nigeria will participate in this transition. The question is whether we will emerge as producers of green solutions or remain consumers of innovations developed elsewhere. With one of the world’s youngest populations, abundant natural resources and significant renewable energy potential, Nigeria possesses the ingredients for a thriving green economy. Yet, potential without deliberate investment is merely an opportunity waiting to be lost. The green transition will create winners and losers. Our responsibility is to ensure that Nigeria’s young people are positioned among the winners. The emerging economy of possibilities Consider the young Nigerian graduate struggling to secure employment while businesses increasingly require solar technicians, environmental scientists, carbon accountants, sustainability analysts and climate-smart agricultural specialists. The jobs are emerging, but are we preparing our young people to occupy them? The World Bank reports that Nigeria’s electrification project created over 5,000 green jobs while expanding access to renewable electricity. Its subsequent $750 million Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) initiative targets improved electricity access for 17.5 million Nigerians. Beyond electricity, these investments create opportunities in equipment manufacturing, installation, maintenance, financing and entrepreneurship. Imagine the economic transformation if Nigerian technical colleges deliberately trained thousands of young people annually to service this expanding market. Across Africa, Kenya’s geothermal energy industry demonstrates how natural resources can support specialised technical employment, while Rwanda’s electric motorcycle ecosystem illustrates the opportunities emerging around cleaner urban transportation. Nigeria cannot afford to watch these developments from the sidelines. From planting trees to creating prosperity My experience designing and implementing reforestation and carbon development projects has reinforced an important lesson: environmental restoration can become a powerful instrument for economic inclusion. A reforestation project is not simply about putting seedlings into the ground. Behind every successfully established forest are opportunities for nursery operators, seed collectors, field technicians, biodiversity specialists, community engagement professionals, digital mapping experts and carbon verification practitioners. In Edo State, large-scale reforestation initiatives are demonstrating how environmental investments can stimulate rural economic activity while restoring degraded ecosystems. However, planting trees without building local capacity risks creating temporary employment rather than sustainable livelihoods. We must deliberately move young Nigerians along the value chain, from casual labour to technical expertise, enterprise ownership and participation in international carbon markets. That is how environmental investment becomes economic transformation. Preparing for the jobs of tomorrow The International Labour Organization’s 2018 projections suggest that appropriate green policies could generate 24 million jobs globally by 2030, while displacing approximately six million existing jobs. These are conditional projections, not guaranteed outcomes. For Nigeria, this presents both an opportunity and a warning. Workers in carbon-intensive industries may face displacement, while those equipped with emerging skills will capture new opportunities. A just transition must therefore protect existing livelihoods while preparing workers for new industries. Our universities, polytechnics and vocational institutions must integrate green skills into mainstream education. Government should establish targeted financing for green enterprises, while businesses must expand apprenticeships, internships and local procurement opportunities. Women and rural youth must not be excluded. Sustainability is also a health imperative. The World Health Organisation estimates that climate change could cause approximately 250,000 additional deaths annually between 2030 and 2050 from selected health risks. Green investments therefore offer multiple dividends: employment, cleaner air, improved health, food security and stronger community resilience. This directly advances the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 3 on health, SDG 4 on education, SDG 7 on clean energy, SDG 8 on decent work and SDG 13 on climate action. The urgency of deliberate action An ancient African proverb reminds us that the best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago; the second-best time is now. The biblical parable of the talents similarly teaches that resources entrusted to us must be developed, not buried. Nigeria’s greatest talent is its people. We must stop treating the green transition exclusively as an environmental obligation and recognise it as an industrial, employment and economic diversification strategy. The countries that prosper tomorrow are those investing in the skills, enterprises and technologies of today. Nigeria must not merely transition to a greener economy. We must build a generation capable of owning it. Our demographic dividend will not materialise automatically. It must be deliberately cultivated. The green economy is coming. The real question is whether Nigeria’s youth will build it, benefit from it, or be left behind. Sarah Esangbedo Ajose-Adeogun is the Founder and Managing Partner of Teasoo Consulting Limited, a leading ESG Strategy and Sustainability Advisory firm committed to helping organisations build resilient, responsible, and future-ready businesses. She is a former community content manager at Shell Petroleum Development Company and a former special adviser on strategy, policy, projects, and performance management to the Government of Edo State. She is the host of the #SarahSpeaks Podcast on YouTube, @WinningBigWithSarah, where she shares practical insights on leadership, ESG, etc. Teasoo Consulting is the developer of ESG Horizon, the first Africentric ESG reporting tool, designed with context-specific ESG reporting aligned with global and local standards.
